opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think turning mathematics into code is one of the most exciting things happening right now, for a few reasons.

First, verifiability. When you write a proof in a formal language like Lean, the computer checks every single step. There's no ambiguity, no "it's obvious that," no gap a referee might miss. For AI, that's huge, because the biggest problem with large language models doing math is that they can sound very convincing while being completely wrong. If the output is formal code, you get a perfect, automatic signal: either the proof compiles or it doesn't. That gives you a reward you can actually trust, which is exactly what you need for reinforcement learning and for scaling up reasoning.

Second, it changes the data problem. Natural-language math on the internet is limited and noisy. Formal math lets a system generate its own attempts, get them verified, and learn from the ones that succeed. So you can build a kind of self-improving loop, where the model proposes, the verifier checks, and the good proofs become new training data. That's very hard to do in informal math.

Third, I think it changes how mathematicians themselves will work. Today, a long, complicated proof might take a community years to fully trust. With formalization, you can collaborate at a much larger scale, because you don't need to personally verify every lemma someone else contributed; the machine does it. AI can then help with the tedious parts, like filling in routine steps and searching libraries, so humans can focus on ideas, intuition, and choosing which questions matter.

Of course, there are real challenges. Formal libraries are still incomplete, autoformalization, translating informal statements into precise code faithfully, is genuinely hard, and you have to make sure the statement you formalized is actually the theorem you meant. But I see math-as-code as a bridge: it connects the creativity of human mathematics with the rigor and scalability of software. And because mathematics underlies so much of science and engineering, getting AI to reason reliably there could be a foundation for trustworthy reasoning much more broadly, even in areas like verified software and hardware.

r002.rationale: It explicitly names verifiability as a benefit and explains that Lean checks proof steps automatically, giving AI a reliable correctness signal.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the value is fundamentally about verification. When you take a mathematical statement and write it in a formal language like Lean, the computer can check every step of the proof. There's no ambiguity, no hand-waving, no "it's obvious that." Either it compiles or it doesn't.

That matters enormously for AI, because right now the biggest problem with large language models in reasoning is that they can produce something that looks right but is subtly wrong. If you ask a model to prove a theorem in natural language, it might give you a very confident, very fluent argument with a gap in the middle. A human expert has to read it carefully to catch that. But if the proof is in Lean, the verifier catches it instantly. So formalization gives you a perfect reward signal. You can train a model, let it generate thousands of attempts, and you know exactly which ones are actually correct. That's something you almost never get in other domains.

The second thing is that mathematics as code becomes composable. Mathlib, the big Lean library, is now hundreds of thousands of theorems that all build on each other. Once a result is formalized, anyone, human or machine, can reuse it without re-deriving it. In natural language math, a lot of knowledge is locked in papers with slightly different notations and assumptions. Code forces consistency.

And I'd say the third thing is more philosophical. Mathematics is in some sense the purest form of reasoning. If we can get AI systems to genuinely do mathematics, not pattern-match but actually construct valid arguments about objects they've never seen, that's strong evidence they can reason in general. So I see math as a kind of testbed. The verifiability makes it the cleanest place to measure progress honestly.

The challenge, of course, is that formalizing is slow and painful for humans. Translating one page of a research paper can take weeks. So part of what we're working on is making that translation itself something AI can help with, so the bottleneck shrinks and the flywheel can actually turn.

r002.rationale: It identifies machine-checkable proof verification as a reason to encode mathematics in Lean for AI, including the ability to tell which generated proofs are correct.

r003.rationale: It mentions Lean as a verifier and Mathlib as a library, but does not raise replacing existing SMT systems with Lean as a possibility to explore.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is that you’re taking something abstract and making it executable—and, in some cases, checkable. In mathematics, a proof can look convincing while hiding a subtle gap. When you formalize it in a system that checks each step, you have to make those assumptions explicit.

For AI, that creates a useful feedback loop. A model can propose an argument, and a verifier can tell it whether the argument actually follows. That doesn’t automatically give you creativity or good mathematical judgment, but it gives you a firmer foundation for exploring ideas.

And the translation itself is interesting. Writing mathematics as code forces you to ask: What exactly do I mean? What does this depend on? I think that precision is valuable both for building better AI and for understanding the mathematics more deeply.

r002.rationale: It says formalizing mathematics in code makes proofs checkable and lets a verifier determine whether an argument follows, identifying verifiability as a benefit for AI.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention SMT systems, Lean, or exploring replacing one with the other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is that code makes mathematical ideas executable and testable. A proof gives you a precise chain of reasoning; turning that reasoning into code forces you to make assumptions and intermediate steps explicit. For AI, that creates a useful connection between generating an answer and checking whether the answer actually follows.

But there’s also a distinction between getting something to run and understanding why it works. Ideally, mathematics and code reinforce each other: mathematics gives us structure and guarantees, while code lets us experiment and see where our intuition breaks down. That feedback loop can help us build AI systems whose reasoning we can inspect and trust more.
